body: Both feet are on the floor and the phone is already in his hand, and the man they belong to is sitting on the edge of a cold bed. The alarm has gone, it is twenty to seven, and there is a window of about four seconds in which two things are equally available. He can open the phone, which he has done every morning since the spring and which will take forty minutes he could not account for. Or he can put it face down on the chest of drawers and go and fill the kettle. Nothing depends on this. Nobody would ever know. He is not aware of choosing anything at all.

That was not a small moment that happens to recur. That was the decision — all of it, made and finished, in less time than it takes to read the sentence describing it. The forty minutes is not the cost. The direction is the cost.

Almost nothing that changes a life arrives labelled as a fork in the road. The turnings are taken at speed, in ordinary clothes, by people thinking about something else, and they are recognised as turnings only from a long way further on.

Take the word decision literally. To decide is to cut — the same root that gives us incision — and the sense is exact: a decision is the removal of everything you are now not going to do. The large ones make the cut visible. You can watch the other job, the other town, the other life closing as you sign. The four-second ones cut nothing you can see. Nothing appears to close, because what is removed is not an option but a degree: a narrowing of what will be easy, or plausible, or even thinkable for you in six months. Do that a thousand times and the fork you eventually arrive at has one usable branch, and you will tell people you had no real choice, and you will be very nearly right.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. Each holds a single frequency permanently, and the schedule is published before it airs rather than assembled around whoever is listening.

Taking this seriously commits a station to something unglamorous. The large decisions announce themselves and get prayed over. The ones that actually set the direction are made in about four seconds, and there is no way to be present for four seconds except by being present for the whole hour that contains them. So the expensive part is not the programming. It is being on at twenty to seven on a wet Tuesday in February, with nothing in particular happening, for somebody who is not listening and could not tell you afterwards what was played.

Everything else competing for that window worked this out long ago. The phone in his hand is not designed to change his mind. It is designed to be the thing his hand reaches for before his mind is involved at all. That is not a conspiracy; it is what happens when an industry is paid by the interval and measures it to the millisecond. The most contested territory in a person is no longer their convictions. It is the four seconds before they have one.

Which is why what is already running matters more than what is available. A frequency sits in the same place every time you tune there, which is the only property that makes a thing reachable inside four seconds. You cannot browse in four seconds. You cannot compare, filter or decide. You can only reach for something your hand already knows the location of, which means a habit, and a habit needs the world to hold still long enough for one to form.
The obvious objection is that this is what deliberate choice is for. Choose better inputs, and the small moments look after themselves.

Be fair to it. A person who selects what they read, keeps a reading plan and picks their music on purpose is doing something real. It works, too, in the deliberate hours — which are not where the direction is set. Every one of those practices requires you to be the person doing the choosing, and the four-second window is defined precisely by your not being that person. You are half asleep, or tired, or in the middle of something else. Curation is a technique for the hours when you are at your best. It has almost nothing to offer the hours when you are not, and those are most of them.
You cannot choose well in a moment you do not know you are in. You can only have arranged, beforehand, what is nearest.

A woman is ironing school shirts at eleven at night, because that is when the ironing happens in that house. She has had the station on low since she came in, the way other people leave a lamp on. She is not listening and could not tell you one thing that has been played. Somewhere in the middle of a song she does not know, she stands the iron up, picks her phone off the worktop and sends a message to her brother, who she has not spoken to since March over something neither of them could now summarise accurately. It takes about eleven seconds. Then she picks the iron back up and does two more shirts. Asked the next morning, she would not connect the two things at all.

Nobody deliberated in that kitchen. Something had been running for two hours at the very edge of her attention, and when the four seconds came, the nearest thing to hand was not the grievance. That is the mechanism, and it is not impressive to look at.

It should be said plainly that this cannot be verified. There will be whole months in which a station running quietly in a house does nothing at all. It will play something jarring at exactly the wrong moment. It is not a technique, it does not produce outcomes on request, and anybody selling it as one is selling something else. A radio station is not a substitute for repentance, counsel or a difficult conversation, all three of which take longer than eleven seconds.

That it cannot be measured is not a weakness in the argument; it is the argument. Anything that could show you its effect on a four-second choice would have to be aiming at that choice, and aiming is exactly what the four seconds refuse. What changes them is not force but nearness, and nearness is built by ordinary repetition over months, in the background, by something that was not trying to catch you. The things that have most changed you were not, at the time, doing anything you noticed.

So the argument is not that music decides anything. It is that by the time the four seconds arrive, the deciding is largely done — done by what is in the room, what has been in the room for a year, and what your hand already knows how to reach. Character is assembled out of moments too small to be discussed, which is why Scripture spends so much less time on dramatic choices than a reader expects, and so much on habits, company, speech and small faithfulness.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not.

The dial carries four kinds of programming. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: clean, entertaining, and playable in a room with children in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international stations, 40 of them across 29 languages, hosted in their own tongues rather than translated into them afterwards.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 376.20 — Melody’s Sparkle. The four-second choices do not happen in the religious hours of your day. They happen at twenty to seven, in the ten minutes in a car park before you go in, at the ironing board at eleven. What is needed there is not a station you would put on to worship, because you will not put that on at twenty to seven. It is a station you can leave running while you are doing nothing in particular and not brace against. That is what this frequency is for: gratitude, family and everyday wonder, clean and warm and never preachy, written to be playable to somebody who is not in church yet. It asks nothing of you at the moment you have nothing to give it, which is the only reason it will still be on in six months.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it nearer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

So treat this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not resolve anything, and do not decide tonight to become a different sort of person by Christmas; that is the large kind of decision, and the large kind is not where you live. Put HM 376.20 on tomorrow at twenty to seven, before the phone is in your hand, and then go and fill the kettle. Leave it running for a month of unremarkable mornings. You will not be able to point to what it did, and that is the strongest thing anybody can honestly say for it.
